Science is limited by the perspective of the scientific community. Generally, objectivity means the state or quality of being true even outside of a subject's individual biases, interpretations, feelings, and imaginings. Science does not satisfy this requirement as it is limited by the interpretation of what's been tested.

In other words, every experiment we've conducted is not the same as every experiment possible. Because of this fact, we are biased in what truths we can interpret. We are doomed to wonder if there's another experiment we haven't thought of yet.

If we identified the color of swans as white for thousands of years, we would reasonably believe that all swans are white, until we met a black swan.

We reasonably believe that all of our scientific theories hold, and though I'm not going to even try to touch their validity/invalidity, I will say that because each and every one of us only has a piece of the knowledge pie, we will be biased and thus not objective.

(Basis of this Argument)

I've mulled it over a bit, and I want to return to my argument and ask if Bayesian inference solves the problem of induction; more importantly, can science be objective using Bayesian inference? I'm going to be a bit arrogant and invite you to assess these questions with me even though the jury seems to be out whether Bayesian Confirmation Theory can be used to confirm hypotheses. Let's look at the sources you've cited.

By definition, knowledge is always tentative and subject to change in these theories of knowledge.

If this is the case, Bayesian inference sounds like a great tool for improving knowledge, but just because what we know isn't contradicted within a 2% margin of error, does this confirm the belief? Using the Dutch Book argument, you could say that it's worth a wager, but though I would bet my life's savings every single time for a white swan given these odds, does it confirm that there are no black swans? Bayesian inference would improve greatly my odds if, after, I found that black swan.

Now a Bayesian will often try to use Bayesian methods to justify the uniformity of nature. We start with a uniform prior so that we haven’t assumed anything about the past or its relevance to the future. Then we merely note that billions of people across thousands of years have only ever observed a uniformity of nature, and hence it is credible to believe the axiom is true.

Even though my gut buys that argument, it is a bit intellectually dishonest. You can never, ever justify an axiom by using a method that relies on that axiom. That is the quintessential begging the question fallacy.

I think the uniformity of nature issue can be dismissed on different grounds. If you want to dismiss an epistemology based on the uniformity of nature issue, then you have to be willing to dismiss every epistemology that allows you to come to knowledge.

This is the reason for my post. This person even sees the issue of using recursive logic, but due to the fear of upsetting the certainty offered by current schools of thought, he accepts the uniformity of nature as an axiom. The uniformity of nature does not stand up to the problem of induction.

Your Stanford source notes that it formalizes inductive logic; it does not touch induction itself in finding truth outside a subject. It even notes a potential problem of this form of knowledge seeking using "the new riddle of induction".

If you cannot solve the problem of induction, you cannot confirm the absolute truth of what comes from science. If you cannot confirm its truth, the practice of science is subjective to the observer.
